title: Learn to Treat Senior Leaders as a Resource and Not as an Authority
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article addresses the common friction of senior leaders inserting themselves into projects they don't fully understand, describing junior leaders' typical response of quietly tolerating an overbearing authority figure. The recommended reframe is to proactively ask senior leaders to serve as a specific resource -- performing a defined task or role -- rather than letting them default into directing traffic broadly. The author argues most senior leaders genuinely want to help and respond well to this framing once it's offered with conviction and specificity. Timing matters: the piece stresses that this reframe works best when offered before a senior leader starts asserting themselves, since redirecting them afterward is much harder.
points: Senior leaders often over-involve themselves in projects, driven by a genuine desire to help and feel relevant.
The recommended fix is proactively asking them to serve as a specific resource rather than letting them direct broadly.
Most senior leaders respond well to this reframe when it's offered with conviction and clear specifics.
Timing matters -- this approach works best offered before a senior leader begins asserting themselves, since redirecting afterward is much harder.
quotes: More seasoned, experienced, and senior leaders often get involved with matters across the organization.
The more powerful tact with senior leaders is to treat them as a resource and ask them to do things that help the situation and the team below them.
When explained with conviction and a detailed set of instructions, asking senior leaders to be a resource makes sense to them.
The key is to accomplish this frame and beat the senior leader to the starting line before a situation or project begins to unfold.
When asked to be a resource to the team and to play a specific role, senior leaders are typically delighted to comply.
